lines.text: Tangent or normal at $x = a$ → point $(a, f(a))$ and gradient $f'(a)$. The normal's gradient is $-\frac{1}{f'(a)}$ (5.4)
Increasing or decreasing → sign of $f'(x)$. Concave-up or concave-down → sign of $f''(x)$. Point of inflexion → $f''(x)$ changes sign (5.2, 5.7, 5.8)
Maximum, minimum or “optimise” → solve $f'(x) = 0$, justify with the sign of $f'$ or of $f''$, and check the end points (5.8)
Product, quotient or function of a function → product, quotient or chain rule (5.6)
Curve from $f'(x)$ and a point → integrate with $+\,C$, substitute the point, solve for $C$ (5.5)
Integrand is a multiple of $g'(x)$ times a function of $g(x)$ → reverse the chain rule, or substitute $u = g(x)$ (5.10)
Area between two curves → integrate top minus bottom between the intersections; split where they cross. Below the $x$-axis → $\int \lvert y\rvert\,\mathrm{d}x$ (5.11)
Velocity or acceleration → differentiate. Displacement from velocity → integrate. Total distance → $\int \lvert v\rvert\,\mathrm{d}t$ (5.9)
Limit of the form $\frac{0}{0}$ or $\frac{\infty}{\infty}$ → l'Hôpital's rule, or Maclaurin series as $x \to 0$ (5.13)
$x$ and $y$ mixed in one equation → implicit differentiation. One rate from another → chain rule linking the rates (5.14)
Product such as $x\mathrm{e}^{x}$ or $x\sin x$, or $\ln x$ on its own → integration by parts, with $u$ the factor that gets simpler when differentiated (5.16)

Differential equation → $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = f(x)g(y)$: separate the variables; $f\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)$: put $y = vx$; $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x)$: integrating factor; an estimate: Euler's method (5.18)
